channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train”: Lumen exposes the throwaway relay chains the China-linked group uses to exploit SD-WAN and IT-management platforms — and lists rail among the sectors targeted
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs published research on 28 October describing “Silent Train”, the framework it says the China-linked group Volt Typhoon has used since November 2023 to reach targets without exposing its own infrastructure. Each operation runs through a fresh chain of typically four to six hops — rented servers outside the US, then compromised small-office routers, IoT devices and enterprise appliances abroad and finally inside the US — which operators can exploit and assemble in under two minutes and clean up afterwards; Lumen counts more than 27 device classes, among them TP-Link routers, Netgear Orbi devices, Fortinet appliances and CyberPanel servers. CyberScoop reports that the group leaned on the framework more after the FBI and Justice Department disrupted its KV botnet in early 2024. The chains are aimed at management and control-plane platforms: Lumen ties the group to exploitation of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN CVE-2026-20127 (CVSS v3.1 10.0, Cisco), seen by late 2025 and continuing after Cisco’s February disclosure; a VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day later designated CVE-2026-16812; N-able N-central CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876; Versa Director in mid-2024; and, with moderate confidence, a Quest KACE zero-day that hit more than 30 victims. Lumen’s key findings name rail among the critical-infrastructure sectors targeted, alongside water, energy, transportation, maritime, aviation and emergency services, and it says it has notified hundreds of victims over three years. It names no victim and gives no count by sector, and neither the report nor coverage by CyberScoop and Zero Day describes access to OT or any operational effect. Black Lotus Labs’ Mike Horka told Zero Day that the researchers agree with US officials’ description of the activity as pre-positioning but see espionage in it too, and that the operators often return using credentials stolen on an earlier visit. These are not the SD-WAN Manager and VeloCloud flaws on this page’s other cards, CVE-2026-76504 and CVE-2026-114625, which no one has attributed to Volt Typhoon; what connects them is that the same orchestration products keep being targeted. It leads because it is a confirmed state campaign whose target list names rail, and the platforms it goes after — SD-WAN orchestrators and IT-management consoles — are the ones that configure the networks at stations, depots, yards and wayside sites (editorial assessment). - Lumen Black Lotus Labs research; corroborated by CyberScoop and Zero Day (Kim Zetter); KEV status of the named CVEs per the CISA catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release) as mirrored by CIRCL; CVSS per Cisco as CNA; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Lumen report and coverage 28 Oct 2026 (Zero Day clarified on 30 Oct that the relay servers were rented, not compromised); activity observed from Nov 2023

item.title: [High] CISA, the FBI and partners say SafePay ransomware has hit at least 600 organizations since August 2024 — through stolen credentials, VPN logins and old firewall flaws
item.category: Advisory — Joint ransomware advisory AA26-293A on an active group; cross-sector, no transport victims named
item.description: The FBI and CISA, with the US Secret Service, Germany’s LKA Rheinland-Pfalz, the UK’s National Crime Agency and the North West Regional Organised Crime Unit, published joint advisory AA26-293A on 20 October. It says SafePay, a closed group that does not use affiliates, has affected at least 600 organizations from multiple critical-infrastructure sectors since August 2024, in North and South America, Europe and Australia, and it gives indicators and techniques observed from November 2024 to August 2026. Entry is through exposed or brute-forced credentials, VPN access — the advisory cites Mullvad VPN addresses — phished accounts and automated exploitation of edge-device flaws; Cybersecurity Dive names CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269, which the CVE records place in Cisco ASA and Firepower Threat Defense software and which CISA lists in KEV with known ransomware use. Once inside, the group steals data before encrypting and hinders recovery by deleting shadow copies and resetting network-attached storage that holds backups. The coverage we read names no transport victim. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: ransomware outages at rail operators typically begin in IT, and remote-access VPNs and NAS-based backups sit in the corporate networks that dispatch, maintenance and passenger-information systems depend on. - Joint advisory AA26-293A as reported by BleepingComputer and Cybersecurity Dive (the CISA page could not be fetched); CVE vendor and KEV details from the CVE records via CIRCL; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Advisory published 20 Oct 2026; reported 21 Oct 2026; activity observed Nov 2024 – Aug 2026

item.title: [High] The FBI and Secret Service say FortiBleed credential theft against FortiGate firewalls is still running — across every critical-infrastructure sector, with no CVE to patch
item.category: Incident — Active credential-theft campaign against boundary firewalls, agency-confirmed, all critical-infrastructure sectors
item.description: The FBI and the US Secret Service issued a joint advisory on Tuesday 6 October warning that the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways remains an active threat. It is not a software vulnerability and has no CVE: per the agencies, it exploits reused or leaked credentials and legacy SHA-256 password storage. Researchers describe credential stuffing and spraying from leak dumps and infostealer logs, offline cracking of extracted password hashes on a GPU cluster, and a Go-based sniffer that passively captures authentication traffic across 24 protocols. Some owners were locked out after the attackers created their own administrator accounts and deleted or reset the legitimate ones. The agencies say compromised firewalls have served as ransomware entry points, and the FBI advisory links the access to Payload ransomware. Cybersecurity Dive reports that targets span all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors — a list that by definition includes transportation systems — naming energy, communications, and food and agriculture among them. The most-cited scale figure, more than 86,644 working device credentials across 194 countries, is SOCRadar’s count as of 19 June, not a new tally; SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments stemming from the access and describes the operator as a Russian-speaking access broker, which is a researcher assessment, not agency attribution. No OT system compromise and no rail victim has been described. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: FortiGate is one of the most common firewalls at the IT/OT boundary of railroads and transit agencies, and a stolen administrator credential there is a way to rewrite segmentation without exploiting anything. - FBI and US Secret Service joint advisory JCSA-20261006-01 (IC3); reported by The Hacker News and Cybersecurity Dive; scale and actor profile per SOCRadar; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Advisory issued 6 Oct 2026; reported 7 Oct 2026; scale figure as of 19 Jun 2026

item.title: [High] Supermarket refrigeration attacks have spread from France to five more European countries — a food-sector campaign, and a direct lesson for contractor-managed station and depot plant
item.category: Incident — Food & retail sector OT attacks in France (Oct) and five more European countries (1–2 Nov); carried here as a cross-sector lesson, not a rail incident
item.description: From the night of 11–12 October, attackers remotely took control of internet-reachable refrigeration management controllers in French supermarkets and forced them into continuous or extended defrost, with setpoints of up to about 50 °C, spoiling stock; the Paris prosecutor reports outbreaks of fire at some sites. A second wave on the night of 12–13 October hit stores with Dixell controllers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on 13 October that about 700 of France’s roughly 10,000 supermarkets were affected, and Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché/Netto and Monoprix have confirmed impact. CERT-FR’s alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 named Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers on 12 October, added Copeland and Dixell xweb on 13 October, and in its 16 October update says attack campaigns are probably still ongoing. As of 2 November CERT-FR’s alert was still at version 3 of 16 October, and no new attack nights, attribution or arrests had been reported in France since 13 October. Danfoss and Copeland say most affected units are older, end-of-life models. No group has claimed the attack, no ransom has been demanded and the entry route has not been established; the national cyber agency ANSSI has mobilised, and the Paris prosecutor’s cybercrime section has opened an inquiry. In October, reports of targeting in other European countries came only from one security firm, Sekoia. On the night of 1–2 November a new wave hit supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia: Ahold Delhaize reported an “IT incident” affecting refrigeration at dozens of Delhaize stores, Colruyt said five franchised Spar shops were attacked, the contractor that runs Delhaize’s refrigeration said evaporators had been switched into defrost, ICA, Coop and Musgrave (SuperValu) reported affected stores, and in Estonia refrigeration supplier Kitman Coldtech said an older Danfoss controller was set to 50°C; no actor has been named and no authority has linked the wave to France. On 29 October Reuters, citing four unnamed officials, reported that US investigators are treating freezer failures at no fewer than six US military commissaries since late August — units forced into defrost, at bases including Fort Huachuca and Fort Irwin — as a suspected cyberattack; Army and Air Force investigators, including an Army cybercrime unit, and US Cyber Command are involved, and one official said investigators had spoken to French police. The Pentagon says it is working with interagency and law-enforcement partners and has not confirmed a cause, and Reuters could not establish whether the commissaries used Danfoss equipment. Separately, Claroty’s Team82 showed on 13 October that an AI coding agent, steered by a researcher, reproduced a previously disclosed Danfoss exploit chain to root in about 28 minutes; it does not say those flaws were used in France. This is not a rail incident and it does not count toward this page’s threat level. It is here as our editorial lesson: stations, depots and tunnels run the same kind of contractor-supported, web-managed plant — HVAC, ventilation, pumping, lighting — and this attack needed little more than reachability and outdated controllers. - CERT-FR alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 (version 3, 16 Oct 2026); AP via News4JAX for the Finance Minister’s figure; SecurityWeek for retailer, vendor, Sekoia and Le Monde details; Claroty Team82 research; Reuters (29 Oct 2026) via The Next Web for the US commissary investigation; rail relevance is our editorial assessment; Reuters, CBS News/AFP, RTÉ and ERR (2 Nov 2026) for the new wave - Attacks on the nights of 11–13 Oct 2026; CERT-FR alert 12 Oct, updated 13 and 16 Oct 2026; Team82 research 13 Oct 2026; US commissary report 29 Oct 2026; new wave in five more countries 1–2 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] ESET documents a Belarus-aligned group’s first destructive attack in Europe — on a Ukrainian manufacturer with an important role in the country’s transportation sector
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Vendor APT reporting; destructive attacks in Ukraine, one victim with a transportation role
item.description: ESET’s APT Activity Report covering April to September 2026, published on 28 October, says that according to its telemetry the Belarus-aligned group it tracks as FrostyNeighbor attacked a manufacturing company in Ukraine that plays an important role in the country’s transportation sector, and calls it the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned actor that ESET has documented in the European theatre. ESET does not name the company, the malware or the date, and describes no effect on transport operations. The same report notes the Iran-aligned OilRig subgroup FilthyFeline taking over activity against a cellular data provider in Uzbekistan, and North Korea’s DeceptiveDevelopment moving from fake job interviews to compromising source-code repositories with stolen developer credentials. Six days earlier, on 22 October, ESET described how the Russia-aligned UAC-0099 gained access to a Ukrainian grain firm through a spearphishing attachment in July 2025, after which Sandworm wiped data there in September 2025 by pushing a deletion tool through Active Directory Group Policy; ESET assesses that UAC-0099 can act as an initial-access group for Sandworm. All attributions are ESET’s assessments. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: transport manufacturers and freight logistics are now inside the destructive-attack target set in this conflict, and a wipe pushed through Group Policy reaches every domain-joined machine, including those that support operations. - ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q3 2026; ESET research on MythicRatatoskr (UAC-0099 and Sandworm); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - MythicRatatoskr research 22 Oct 2026 (intrusion Jul–Sep 2025); APT Activity Report 28 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] US authorities seize the scanning and phishing tools of a China-based contractor whose named targets included airports in Japan and Poland and a US power company
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Nation-state-linked tooling disrupted; transportation hubs among named targets
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced on 8 October court-authorised seizures, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, of domains behind two tools: Microscan, a Python web application carrying more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts, and FishHub, a spear-phishing and malware-delivery service. US authorities tie both to Integrity Technology Group, a China-based company sanctioned last year. CyberScoop describes the tools as Flax Typhoon-linked, while Cybersecurity Dive says the activity mimics that group and others such as Ethereal Panda rather than equating them. A Mirai-variant IoT botnet supported Microscan, and a joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory notes persistence through VPN software. Court documents name Microscan targets including a South Carolina power company, airports in Japan and Poland, gas and power companies in Taiwan and a multinational NGO, with Taiwanese universities hit by FishHub phishing; no target’s compromise is confirmed. CISA’s Chris Butera said Chinese government-affiliated actors continue to position themselves within critical-infrastructure networks, including operational technology systems. No rail operator is named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: transportation hubs are on the target list, and pre-positioning of this kind typically starts with exactly what Microscan automated — scanning internet-facing services for known flaws. - DOJ and FBI seizure announcement and joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory, as reported by CyberScoop and Cybersecurity Dive; target list from court documents per Cybersecurity Dive; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Seizures announced 8 Oct 2026; reported 8–9 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Mandiant says ShinyHunters is back exploiting Oracle PeopleSoft by encoding one letter past WAF rules — transportation is among the sectors with compromised systems
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Mass exploitation of an enterprise application, transportation among sectors hit
item.description: Google Threat Intelligence and Mandiant reported on 25 September a renewed mass-exploitation campaign by UNC6240, the group known as ShinyHunters, against CVE-2026-35273, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (the /PSEMHUB/ path), rated CVSS v3.1 9.8. The flaw was first exploited as a zero-day against academic institutions in late May and early June, and Oracle has had a fix out since June. The new wave requests /%50SEMHUB/ instead: WAF rules that match the literal path miss it, and WebLogic decodes and routes the request anyway, reaching, in Mandiant’s words, “systems whose operators may have believed their WAF rules had mitigated the exposure”. Mandiant counts “dozens of systems” compromised globally across higher education, technology and IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government, names no victims, and says it has notified more than 100 organisations whose addresses matched vulnerable endpoints. The tooling includes JSP web shells, Neo-reGeorg tunnels, a SIDEEYE backdoor delivered in a trojanised Light Alloy media-player installer, and MeshAgent. CISA has listed CVE-2026-35273 in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue since 12 June 2026 and marks it as known to be used in ransomware campaigns. Since then the FBI has said, on 6 October, that a breach of its own jobs portal resulted from a contractor that failed to apply a patch explicitly issued for the platform — which Reuters, citing unnamed sources, identified as Oracle PeopleSoft — and on 9 October it announced another arrest of a suspected ShinyHunters member, saying the group has breached more than 140 organisations. Oracle’s October 2026 quarterly Critical Patch Update has since been released. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: many transit authorities and railroads run PeopleSoft for HR, payroll and finance, and a web shell on that tier puts employee records and whatever directory and database credentials the application holds within an attacker’s reach. It is an IT-side risk, not an OT one. - Google Threat Intelligence / Mandiant report; corroborated by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News; FBI statements as reported by The Hacker News, with the platform identification attributed to Reuters’ unnamed sources; CVSS v3.1 score per the published CVE record and KEV status per the CISA catalogue; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Mandiant report 25 Sep 2026; FBI statements 6 Oct and 9 Oct 2026; KEV-listed 12 Jun 2026

item.title: [Low] Nozomi’s summer OT telemetry ranks transportation second for alerts per customer, behind manufacturing
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Vendor OT/IoT telemetry; transportation ranked second
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published its June–August 2026 OT and IoT telemetry review on 12 October. Ranked by alerts per organisation, manufacturing came first, transportation second and energy, utilities and waste third, displacing government. Credential-related techniques made up roughly a third of detections. Among alerts Nozomi could attribute to an actor, Scattered Spider accounted for close to half, and Russia-linked or Russian-speaking actors together for more than a third. Siemens PLCs and Rockwell products were among the most-detected vulnerable products, and Nozomi says 58 percent of 2026 vulnerabilities rate High or Critical, up from 48 percent in 2025. Two cautions apply: alerts per organisation measures what Nozomi customers’ sensors flagged, not a count of attacks, and the actor names are telemetry attributions, not confirmed intrusions. The report does not break out rail. The reading for rail is our editorial assessment: transportation’s place in the ranking reflects a sector whose networks are increasingly instrumented and noisy, and the credential share supports putting identity controls ahead of exotic OT exploits. - Nozomi Networks Labs blog; figures are Nozomi’s customer telemetry; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 12 Oct 2026; data June–August 2026

item.title: [Info] Dragos sees old worms — Sality, Conficker, WannaCry — turning up more often in OT incident calls, and warns the wrong cleanup can hurt more than the infection
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Vendor incident-response observation and cleanup guidance
item.description: Dragos’s Lesley Carhart and Jan Hoff wrote on 15 October that requests for help with legacy commodity malware such as Sality, Gammima, WannaCry and Conficker have risen sharply in recent years, and that many OT networks Dragos is called into carry between 20 and 70 distinct commodity-malware variants across several subnets, often on systems older than Windows XP Service Pack 2. They attribute the rise to more networking and remote access, better visibility, and regulation that expects critical-infrastructure networks to be clean. Their answer is a “Now / Next / Never” framework, with a white paper, for deciding what to clean immediately, what to schedule and what to leave contained, and a warning that the wrong cleanup can be riskier than the infection itself. No actor or campaign is involved. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: signalling-support, SCADA and passenger-information estates are full of long-lived Windows hosts that suppliers certify and operators cannot simply rebuild, which is exactly the population Dragos describes. - Dragos blog; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] DOE and Idaho National Laboratory start a weekly Cyber-Informed Engineering series — rail’s fail-safe tradition is the same idea, applied on purpose
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Federal engineering-practice series, voluntary
item.description: The Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) and Idaho National Laboratory announced on 13 October a weekly “CIE Back-to-School” series that works through the twelve principles of Cyber-Informed Engineering one at a time, each with an overview, a case study and questions for engineers, starting with consequence-focused design. A new, simplified CIE Handbook is due at the end of the series. The argument behind CIE is that the security question belongs upstream, in design: identify the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineer them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system staying trustworthy. The series is aimed at energy infrastructure and is voluntary guidance, not regulation. The rail connection is our editorial assessment. Interlocking, fail-safe signalling and vital logic exist precisely so that an upstream failure cannot produce an unsafe movement; CIE asks that those principles be applied deliberately to newer digital systems rather than assumed to still hold. It is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - DOE CESER and Idaho National Laboratory announcement, as reported by Industrial Cyber; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Series announced 13 Oct 2026; reported 14 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] PHP2Shell: an attacker chained the PHP flaws with a Linux kernel bug to take root on about two dozen PAN-OS firewalls — every supported branch now has a hotfix, and Siemens’ RUGGEDCOM APE1808 still patches through support
item.category: Critical Advisory — Boundary firewall, confirmed root compromises, KEV-listed; no rail victim
item.description: Exploitation of PHP2Shell, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS v4.0 9.2, PHP Group), has moved from honeypots to real victims. Palo Alto Networks’ advisory, Critical since 27 October, reports active exploitation of PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet — the web interface and XML API on PA-Series, VM-Series and Panorama; GlobalProtect is not affected — and by 29 October hotfixes were out for every supported branch. On 29 October Palo Alto’s Unit 42 said it had independently verified research by Dream: an attacker chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation flaw, which The Record and Infosecurity Magazine identify as CVE-2026-46300, to gain root on about two dozen PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October, with victims in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea. The attacker reportedly took credentials, private keys, network topology and full Active Directory user and group listings, and pursued one US government-affiliated environment further. Dream attributes the campaign to a suspected China-nexus actor; Palo Alto names no actor. Unit 42 says about 0.02% of Palo Alto’s global installed base had internet-facing management interfaces configured and was affected, that each affected customer has been contacted, and that the fixes interrupt the observed chain; GreyNoise has counted at least six successful exploitations. CISA listed the PHP flaws in KEV on 26 October and the kernel flaw on 28 October (see the next card). Siemens’ SSA-566512 lists RUGGEDCOM APE1808, an application module for Siemens’ ruggedised RUGGEDCOM platform that can host a Palo Alto firewall, as affected when it runs PAN-OS 10.2 to 12.2; its 28 October revision to V1.1 is administrative, and fixes still come through Siemens customer support. No OT operator is named, no rail or transit victim has been reported and no APE1808 exploitation has been reported. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: this is confirmed root on the firewall class that guards many railway IT/OT boundaries, including a ruggedised Siemens variant built for communications rooms, substations and trackside cabinets, and the attacker went straight from the firewall to the directory that unlocks what sits behind it. - Palo Alto Networks advisory CVE-2026-109618 (Critical since 27 Oct, last updated 29 Oct 2026); Unit 42 threat brief; Dream research as reported by The Record and Infosecurity Magazine; Siemens ProductCERT SSA-566512 (V1.1); CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release); CVSS per the PHP Group as CNA; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Root compromises 23–24 Oct 2026; KEV listing 26 Oct 2026; Siemens V1.1 28 Oct 2026; Unit 42 confirmation and remaining PAN-OS hotfixes 29 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] The Linux kernel flaw used to root those firewalls, CVE-2026-46300, is in KEV — and Siemens lists it in the Linux subsystem of S7-1500 MFP controllers, fixed in V3.1.7 but not for V3.1.5
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited Linux kernel privilege escalation, KEV-listed; OT bridge through Siemens S7-1500 MFP; local access required
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel flaw that Infosecurity Magazine and Cybersecurity Dive call “Fragnesia”, to KEV on 28 October with a 31 October federal deadline. When the kernel coalesces network-buffer fragments it can drop a marker that says they are shared, so ESP decryption runs in place over page-cache data and a low-privileged local user can write to the cached contents of files they should only be able to read, potentially gaining root. Red Hat scores it CVSS v3.1 7.8, and it is fixed upstream in 5.10.257, 5.15.208, 6.1.174, 6.6.141, 6.12.91, 6.18.33 and 7.0.10. CISA’s KEV entry says it can be chained with the PHP2Shell flaws to plant PHP web shells and run commands as root, and The Record and Infosecurity identify it as the kernel step in the PAN-OS compromises described in the previous card. On its own it is a local flaw: it does not let anyone in from the network, but it turns any foothold into root. The OT bridge is Siemens. Its advisories SSA-019113 and SSA-082556 cover the additional GNU/Linux subsystem of the SIMATIC S7-1500 CPU 1518(F)-4 PN/DP MFP: Siemens lists CVE-2026-46300 for V3.1.6, fixed by updating to V3.1.7 or later, while V3.1.5 has no fix and is no longer maintained, leaving Siemens’ mitigations of running only trusted applications and restricting access to the Linux subsystem’s shell. No exploitation of a Siemens product has been reported. Keep it separate from CVE-2026-43284, a similar kernel flaw with public exploit code listed in Hitachi Energy’s CoreTec advisory, which is not in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: S7-1500 controllers run depot, workshop, tunnel-ventilation and station plant, and many trackside, telemetry and on-board gateways run embedded Linux, where a flaw like this turns a low-privileged foothold into full control of the device. - CISA KEV entry and CVE record via CIRCL (30 Oct 2026 catalogue); Siemens ProductCERT SSA-019113 and SSA-082556; chain reporting by The Record and Infosecurity Magazine; CVSS per Red Hat; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - CVE published 23 May 2026; added to KEV 28 Oct 2026; named in the PAN-OS chain 29 Oct 2026; federal due date 31 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Cisco ASA and FTD: an exploited zero-day lets an unauthenticated attacker reload the remote-access VPN firewall — in KEV with a 1 November deadline and no workaround
item.category: Critical Advisory — Boundary firewall and remote-access VPN, exploited denial-of-service zero-day, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75 on 28 October for CVE-2026-76418 in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) software, and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October. Where SSL VPN is enabled and a tunnel group — DefaultWEBVPNGroup included — is configured with secondary authentication, a crafted request from a remote, unauthenticated attacker makes the device reload; Cisco notes that a successful VPN login is not needed to reach the vulnerable code. Cisco scores it CVSS v3.1 8.6. It is a denial of service, not code execution, but each reload drops every VPN session and whatever else the firewall carries until it restarts. There are no workarounds: Cisco’s mitigation is to disable the tunnel-group list or remove secondary authentication, which it says weakens the VPN’s security. Fixed releases are ASA 9.16.4.104, 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48 and 9.24.1.27 or 9.24.10.1, and FTD 7.0.11, 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 and 10.1.1. CISA added it to KEV on 29 October with a 1 November federal deadline. Cisco has not named the attackers or described targets, and no rail or transit victim has been reported. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: ASA and FTD are common at railway IT/OT boundaries and as the VPN that remote engineers and suppliers use, secondary authentication is exactly the stronger login operators add for that access, and older ASA and FTD flaws are among the entry routes in the SafePay advisory on this page. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75 (v1.0); CISA KEV entry via the CVE record on CIRCL (30 Oct 2026 catalogue); The Hacker News; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Advisory 28 Oct 2026; added to KEV 29 Oct 2026; federal due date 1 Nov 2026

item.title: [Critical] Arista patches a third exploited VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day in four months, and CISA adds it to KEV — the console that configures the SD-WAN edge at every connected site
item.category: Critical Advisory — SD-WAN orchestrator, vendor-confirmed exploited zero-day; in KEV since 23 Oct
item.description: Arista disclosed on 22 October that CVE-2026-114625, an SQL injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator, was detected by Arista and is known to be actively exploited. Any authenticated user, down to the lowest built-in tenant role, can use it to gain operator privileges and act as a local “superuser operator”. Arista, as CVE numbering authority, rates it CVSS v3.1 9.9 and v4.0 9.4. Fixed releases are 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12; Arista-hosted and dedicated orchestrators are already patched, and VeloCloud gateways and edges are not affected. SecurityWeek lists two IP addresses seen in the attacks and quotes Arista: “There is no configuration that can prevent the exposure,” so updating is the remedy. It is the third exploited orchestrator zero-day in four months, after CVE-2026-16812 in July and CVE-2026-93952 in September, and CISA added it to KEV late on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, which has passed; an earlier edition of this page wrongly showed it as not listed. No victims, sectors or actor have been named for CVE-2026-114625; Lumen’s Silent Train report, this edition’s top story, ties Volt Typhoon to the July flaw, CVE-2026-16812, not to this one. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: where stations, depots and wayside sites hang off an SD-WAN, the orchestrator holds the configuration of every edge, so whoever controls it can reroute traffic or open paths into the networks behind them. - Arista security advisory 0199 as reflected in the CVE record (Arista as CNA) and reported by SecurityWeek and The Hacker News; CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Disclosed and patched 22 Oct 2026; added to KEV 23 Oct 2026; earlier exploited VCO zero-days July and Sept 2026

item.title: [High] Siemens confirms its signed Software Center program is being abused to plant malware on Windows PCs, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited OT-vendor software, KEV-listed, ClickFix abuse; no rail victim
item.description: Siemens said on 19 October that CVE-2026-110936, a DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens Software Center — the program that downloads, installs, activates and updates Siemens software customers have bought — is being exploited. Attackers bundle a genuine, validly signed copy of version 3.5.8.7 with their own DLLs in an installer pushed through ClickFix lures, so the trusted program runs the attackers’ code; Siemens tells customers to look for it even on PCs where Software Center was never installed. Siemens links the activity to the “Romulus” ClickFix campaign, names no malware family, and says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached to its knowledge. Version 4.0.9.8 fixes the flaw. CISA added it to KEV on 20 October, due 3 November, and republished the advisory on 22 October with Transportation Systems among the listed sectors. As of 31 October Siemens’ advisory was still at version 1.2 and we found no newer campaign reporting. No rail victim has been reported. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: engineering workstations that trust anything Siemens-signed are exactly what this abuses, and the federal deadline is 3 November. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-580366 (V1.2, 19 Oct 2026) and its active-exploitation notice; CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release); CISA ICSA-26-295-03, read via CISA’s CSAF data as mirrored by CIRCL; SecurityWeek; the allow-listing and rail points are our editorial assessment - Advisory 15 Oct 2026; exploitation confirmed 19 Oct 2026; added to KEV 20 Oct 2026; CISA republication 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] PHP2Shell in industrial products: Cisco’s URWB wireless, which rail operators use for train-control links, awaits a November fix; Siemens now lists affected grid-control software; ABB says one gateway line will never be fixed
item.category: Advisory — KEV-listed PHP flaws in industrial software and wireless; vendor notices, fixes partial; no OT product compromise reported
item.description: Industrial vendors are still mapping the PHP flaws CISA listed in KEV on 26 October (the PAN-OS firewall compromises have their own card above). The most rail-relevant new entry is Cisco’s: its PHP advisory, at version 1.10 on 30 October, lists Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul (URWB) and Unified Industrial Wireless Software as vulnerable, with fixed release 26.2.1.9 expected in November 2026 and a workaround described in bug CSCwx37073. For this product the attacker must be authenticated as an administrator, which Cisco says lowers the score to CVSS v3.1 6.6, and Cisco says it knows of no malicious use against its products. Cisco’s own product material says rail organisations use URWB to connect applications such as Communications-Based Train Control. Siemens’ SSA-166980, at version 1.2 since 29 October, now lists affected products: AMIS TS, blueplanet 360, Energy Engage and the Spectrum Power 3, 4, 7 and TG grid-control family. Several have no fix — AMIS TS, blueplanet 360, Spectrum Power 4 and Energy Engage V2.0SP9 — while Spectrum Power 3 and 7 take Red Hat’s PHP patch, Spectrum Power TG an upgrade to PHP 8.5.12 and Energy Engage V3.1SP1 PHP 8.1.34 release 6; Desigo, Climatix, Siveillance and SiPass remain listed as not affected. That corrects our earlier statement that SSA-166980 listed only not-affected products. Schneider Electric’s SESB-2026-295-01, now version 3.2.0 (30 October), added the EcoStruxure Foxboro DCS H90 Server on 28 October with port blocking as the only mitigation, alongside the existing EcoStruxure Control Engineering remediation, Security Expert 1.48.4.0 and LINEoptimize through ProLeiT support. ABB published three more notices: Netcontrol 100, 200 and 500 RTUs and NAM (30 October, no fix yet), ASPECT-Enterprise, NEXUS and MAT-x devices (29 October, no firmware fix at publication), and the Arctic ARG, ARP, ARR, ARC and ARM600 wireless gateways (30 October), which are obsolete and which ABB says it will not fix. Those three score CVE-2026-109619 at CVSS v3.1 8.1; ABB’s APROL advisory SA26P015 scores both flaws 9.8, and ABB had not published the planned APROL patch as of 31 October. Rockwell’s SD1802 still confirms no affected products, and Moxa’s response notice MPSA-260001 (22 October) says no Moxa product is affected. No compromise of an OT or industrial-wireless product has been reported. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: URWB carries train-to-wayside links on some railways, Arctic-class cellular gateways and Netcontrol-class RTUs turn up in traction-power and remote telemetry, and grid-control software of the Spectrum Power kind can sit in the energy control rooms that supply traction power. - Cisco advisory cisco-sa-php-october26-Jj384Daq (v1.10) and Cisco’s URWB solution overview; Siemens ProductCERT SSA-166980 (V1.2); Schneider Electric SESB-2026-295-01 (v3.2.0); ABB advisories 2NGA003256, 2NGA003224, 9AKK108473A4963 and SA26P015 (CSAF data via db.gcve.eu and ABB PSIRT); Rockwell Automation SD1802; Moxa MPSA-260001; CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - PHP fixes 21 Oct 2026; Moxa notice 22 Oct 2026; KEV 26 Oct 2026; Schneider v3.0.0 28 Oct 2026; Siemens SSA-166980 V1.2 and ABB ASPECT 29 Oct 2026; ABB Netcontrol and Arctic, Schneider v3.2.0 and Cisco v1.10 30 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa fixes a man-in-the-middle flaw in its Remote Connect client — but its OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway is end-of-life, with static keys and an SMS command-injection flaw that will not be fixed
item.category: Advisory — Remote-access client and cellular gateway flaws; one product end-of-life with no fix; no reported exploitation
item.description: Moxa published advisory MPSA-269510 on 27 October for three flaws. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, Moxa) affects the MRC Client of Moxa Remote Connect Suite, versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0: because the client does not properly validate certificates when it takes an OpenVPN configuration supplied by the server, an attacker positioned between client and server could impersonate the server and read or alter the connection. Version 4.2.2 is not affected and, according to CERT-FR, the fix is obtained through Moxa technical support. The other two affect the OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway: CVE-2026-111460 (v4.0 7.7), private keys for HTTPS and the device certificate authority embedded statically in the firmware, and CVE-2026-111461 (v4.0 7.5), an operating-system command injection that an attacker with the required privileges can reach when SMS management is enabled. The gateway is end-of-life and no fix will be issued; Moxa’s mitigations are to reset the device so it regenerates its keys and to keep SMS management disabled, which is the default. No exploitation has been reported, and none of the three is in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: Moxa networking and cellular equipment is common across railways — on rolling stock, at stations and in wayside and telemetry cabinets — and remote-access clients like MRC are how engineers reach those sites from outside. - Moxa security advisory MPSA-269510; CVE records with Moxa as CNA, via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-AVI-1393 for end-of-life status and fix distribution; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Fortinet has shipped fixes for critical and high-severity flaws in FortiOS, FortiManager and three other products — with CVE details held back until 10 November
item.category: Advisory — Boundary-firewall and management fixes released ahead of disclosure; vendor-confirmed; no reported exploitation
item.description: WaterISAC reported in a TLP:CLEAR notification on 27 October that Fortinet has released a coordinated set of updates for critical and high-severity vulnerabilities in FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, found through Fortinet’s AI-assisted security testing. CVE identifiers, scores and technical details are due with public advisories on Fortinet’s PSIRT page on 10 November; until then, scanners that work from CVEs will not flag affected devices, so WaterISAC advises checking firmware versions directly. The fixed releases it lists are FortiOS 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.14; FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 and 7.2.13; FortiMail 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9; and FortiAuthenticator 8.0.4 and 6.6.11. WaterISAC says no active exploitation has been reported. Fortinet’s own announcement, a 21 October blog post by its chief information security officer, Carl Windsor, lists the same fixed releases, says the issues were found through AI-assisted testing and says advisories will be published on 10 November; it does not report exploitation. Our previous edition wrongly said no Fortinet publication existed. No CVE or score is given here because none has been published. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: FortiGate is among the most common firewalls at railway IT/OT boundaries, FortiManager is how many managed providers run them (see the Peerstitch card), and the gap between fixes and disclosure is time in which attackers can compare old and new builds. - Fortinet CISO blog post; WaterISAC TLP:CLEAR vulnerability notification; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Fortinet announcement 21 Oct 2026; FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer builds 22 Oct 2026; WaterISAC notification 27 Oct 2026; CVE details due 10 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] The FortiOS flaw behind Unit 42’s Peerstitch case is in KEV — attackers reached it through a provider’s FortiManager and exposed more than 500 managed firewalls
item.category: Critical Advisory — Firewall management chain, exploited and KEV-listed; managed-service-provider intrusion
item.description: CISA added CVE-2025-61624, a path-traversal flaw in the FortiOS command-line interface that also affects FortiProxy, FortiPAM and FortiSwitchManager, to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October federal deadline. Fortinet rates it Medium because the attacker needs privileged, authenticated access; it fixed the flaw in April 2026 and now marks it known exploited. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reported on 14 October how it was used: at a telecommunications managed service provider, attackers exploited FortiManager CVE-2024-47575 and took configurations, serial numbers and credential material for more than 500 managed FortiGates, then used CVE-2025-61624 to gain root on managed firewalls and drop a loader Unit 42 calls PEERSTITCH with an SSH reverse-shell back door. Unit 42 describes the 500-plus as exposure of configuration and credential material, not confirmed intrusion into the provider’s customers. It tracks the cluster as CL-STA-0954 (UNC5820), notes overlaps with suspected nation-state intrusions and names no state. The CVE record also lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808, an industrial appliance that runs Fortinet’s firewall software. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: station and depot firewalls are often run by a managed provider through FortiManager, which makes the provider’s management plane part of your boundary. - Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 report (14 Oct 2026); Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-122; CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release); CVE record via CIRCL for the RUGGEDCOM APE1808 entry; The Hacker News; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Unit 42 report 14 Oct 2026; added to KEV 16 Oct 2026; fix released Apr 2026

item.title: [Critical] Ivanti Connect Secure: CISA adds the root-escalation link, CVE-2026-111357, and a second chain flaw to KEV — due 2 and 13 November, with the fix for the whole chain still to be confirmed
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access VPN, exploited three-flaw chain, all three CVEs now in KEV; correction
item.description: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that CVE-2026-104935 in Connect Secure had been exploited against a limited number of customers: an authentication bypass by spoofing and a file write that together let a remote, unauthenticated attacker run commands (CVSS v3.1 8.6, Ivanti). Volexity, which found the activity during an incident response, said the attackers added a privilege escalation to reach root on fully patched appliances; Volexity’s case begins on 3 October and Defused saw activity from 1 October. The operator, which Volexity tracks as UTA0576, stole LDAP and domain credentials, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, Kerberoasted, sprayed passwords and wiped the appliance’s logs; Volexity has only low confidence that the motive is criminal rather than espionage. On 30 October CISA added two more Connect Secure flaws to KEV and says both can be chained with CVE-2026-104935: CVE-2026-111357, in which the dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data, allowing escalation to root (CVSS v3.1 7.0, MITRE as CNA; federal due date 2 November), and CVE-2026-118527, which KEV lists as a predictable-identifier flaw (due 13 November). Correction: earlier editions of this page said the privilege-escalation link had no CVE and no patch; the record for CVE-2026-111357 has been public since 15 October, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security listed it as exploited in an update on 16 October. The fix for the whole chain is not verified: 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1 fix CVE-2026-104935, but NVD lists versions up to 22.8R2.5 and 25.1.x before 25.1.1.3 as affected by CVE-2026-111357, so check Ivanti’s advisory for the build that fixes it. CISA, like Volexity, warns that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect this compromise, because the chain patches code in memory and restores configuration. No rail or transit victim has been named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: Connect Secure is a common VPN for contractors and remote engineers, and this actor went straight for the directory credentials that unlock what sits behind it. - Ivanti advisory as reflected in the CVE records; Volexity research; CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release) and the CVE-2026-111357 record via CIRCL; Canadian Centre for Cyber Security AV26-1035; reported by SecurityWeek, CyberScoop and Cybersecurity Dive (Defused data); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Disclosed and KEV-listed 13 Oct 2026; CVE-2026-111357 published 15 Oct 2026; two more chain CVEs added to KEV 30 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] NetScaler: a fourth critical SAML flaw lands on top of three exploited zero-days — builds that fixed September’s bugs need upgrading again, and patching does not evict an intruder
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access gateway, three exploited zero-days in KEV plus a fourth critical flaw
item.description: Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-107406 in bulletin CTX697191 on the evening of 8 October, and it was widely reported on 9 October: a memory overflow in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider, which Citrix says may lead to remote code execution or denial of service. It is rated CVSS v4.0 9.5, there is no workaround, Citrix says it is not aware of exploitation, and it was not in KEV as of CISA’s 30 October catalogue. The catch is the builds many operators installed in the past three weeks: as reported from Citrix’s bulletin, 14.1-73.37 to 14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.23 to 13.1-64.28 remain vulnerable when the appliance acts as a SAML identity provider, so those must be upgraded again, to 14.1-73.46 or 13.1-64.29 or later (FIPS and NDcPP builds are listed separately). In guidance reported on 12 October, CISA urged customers to patch, warned that attackers use the crash bug CVE-2026-88779 to force reboots so that code planted through CVE-2026-88771 runs, and released detection rules. That sits on top of the exploited trio already in KEV: CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, each CVSS v4 9.5 and listed on 27 September, and CVE-2026-88779, listed on 4 October, which Citrix and watchTowr describe as denial of service. Mandiant ties the campaign to suspected state-nexus actors, names no group and counts dozens of affected organisations in North America and Europe; Arctic Wolf’s figure of at least 78 counts targeted organisations, not confirmed victims; Shadowserver sees more than 20,000 exposed or potentially vulnerable appliances. Reported post-exploitation tooling includes custom PHP web shells, and Mandiant warns that upgrading alone does not remove access an intruder already has. No rail or transit victim has been named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for supplier and remote-engineer access, and on many railways and transit agencies it is the path by which signalling, SCADA and fare-system contractors reach the OT DMZ. - Citrix bulletins CTX697174 and CTX697191; CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release); CISA guidance, Mandiant, Arctic Wolf and Shadowserver figures via Cybersecurity Dive; SAML build details via The Hacker News and iTnews; watchTowr via SecurityWeek; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Exploited trio KEV-listed 27 Sep and 4 Oct 2026; CVE-2026-107406 disclosed 8 Oct 2026; CISA patch guidance reported 12 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] A suspected PRC-nexus actor exploited a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day from late August — now in KEV, and the kind of console suppliers use to reach plant PCs
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-support appliance, exploited zero-day, suspected state-nexus actor, in KEV
item.description: BeyondTrust and Google Threat Intelligence Group disclosed on 15 October that CVE-2026-102764, a flaw in Remote Support’s internal messaging components that lets attackers perform file operations on the appliance, had been exploited as a zero-day since late August. BeyondTrust, as CVE numbering authority, scores it CVSS v4.0 9.3, and every Remote Support release up to 26.2.3 is affected. GTIG attributes the exploitation, and the follow-on SAWFLY web shell and BARECLAW tunneller, to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor it tracks as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221), on the basis of tooling and tradecraft overlap. SecurityWeek reports two appliances compromised, one hosted by BeyondTrust and one self-hosted; the attackers gained root, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the tool’s file transfer to pull documents from users’ desktops. BeyondTrust shipped a fix, patch BT26-05-RS, on 8 October and had patched its SaaS customers by 9 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand, and releases older than 24.3.1 must be upgraded first. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 16 October with a federal deadline of 19 October, which has passed. GTIG names no victims or sectors. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: remote-support consoles of this kind are how many signalling, SCADA and building-systems suppliers reach the engineering workstations they commissioned, and a console under someone else’s control reaches everything its sessions do. - Google Threat Intelligence Group report; BeyondTrust advisory BT26-05 as reflected in the CVE record and reported by SecurityWeek; CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Disclosed 15 Oct 2026; added to KEV 16 Oct 2026; fix shipped 8 Oct 2026; exploitation from late Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Six more exploited flaws enter KEV in three days — PAN-OS management, Cisco’s email gateway, a Windows Mark-of-the-Web bypass, AhsayCBS backup and Atlassian Data Center
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, firewall management, email gateway, Windows, backup and collaboration servers
item.description: Beyond Ivanti, CISA added six exploited flaws to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 13, 14 and 15 October, each with a three-day federal deadline. CVE-2026-96951, listed on 13 October, is the exploited zero-day in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday: a Windows Shell security-feature bypass that evades Mark of the Web, so downloaded files run without the usual warning; it needs user interaction and is scored CVSS v3.1 8.8. The release as a whole fixed more than 1,400 CVEs. CVE-2026-0322, listed on 14 October, lets an authenticated attacker with network access to the PAN-OS management interface run code as root on PA-Series, VM-Series and Panorama (CVSS v4.0 8.6 per Palo Alto); Palo Alto reports very limited exploitation and published attacker IP addresses. CVE-2026-76519, also 14 October and scored CVSS 9.8 by Cisco, lets an unauthenticated sender write files and run commands as root on Cisco Secure Email Gateway through a crafted attachment, where file reputation is enabled on a mail policy and Content Scanner Tools are older than 25.3.0.5525; it is the second exploited flaw in that product in a month. AhsayCBS CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134, listed the same day, chain an authentication flaw and a command injection in a backup server; Huntress saw them used to plant web shells and cryptocurrency miners, and Ahsay says its August patches were incomplete. CVE-2026-21589, listed on 15 October, lets an unauthenticated attacker read known files from the web root of Atlassian Data Center products including Confluence, Jira and Bitbucket. On 8 October CISA had also listed five much older flaws, in ISC BIND, Apache Struts, Strapi, ONLYOFFICE Docs and ProFTPD. No rail victim is named in any of these. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: PAN-OS often sits at the IT/OT boundary, Windows engineering workstations and HMIs are where a Mark-of-the-Web bypass lands, and the backup server is what a ransomware crew wants to own before it encrypts. - CISA KEV catalogue (15 Oct 2026 release); Palo Alto Networks and Cisco advisories; vendor details as reflected in the CVE records; Microsoft Patch Tuesday via SecurityWeek; AhsayCBS via The Hacker News (Huntress research); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - KEV additions 8, 13, 14 and 15 Oct 2026; federal deadlines 11–18 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] SonicWall SMA1000: a CVSS 10 pre-authentication flaw drew exploitation attempts within two days of the fix — not in KEV, and not a confirmed breach
item.category: Advisory — Secure-access gateway, CVSS 10, exploitation attempts, not KEV-listed
item.description: SonicWall published advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 on 6–7 October for CVE-2026-102255, a server-side request forgery in the WorkPlace interface of SMA1000 secure-access appliances (SMA 6210, 7210 and 8200v). Reached through an unintended alternate path, it lets an unauthenticated attacker make the appliance send requests to its own internal functions; CISA’s enrichment scores it CVSS v3.1 10.0, and SonicWall calls it maximum severity. The same release fixed three authenticated flaws: CVE-2026-102256, an administrator command injection; CVE-2026-102257, a Zip Slip in the management console; and CVE-2026-102258, a stored cross-site scripting bug. Defused saw its first hits on SMA1000 decoys on 8 October, and Previdian counted 135 attempts from two US addresses. Those are attempts against sensors: no source has established a successful breach of a customer network, and the CVE was not in KEV as of CISA’s 30 October catalogue; some threat feeds now mark it as exploited, but no source has confirmed that. Fixed builds are 12.4.3-03670 and 12.5.0-03082 or later; there is no workaround, and SMA 100 and firewall SSL VPN are not affected. SMA1000 has been exploited repeatedly in 2026, so attempts this fast are not a surprise. No rail victim is named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: SMA1000 is a secure-access gateway of the kind suppliers and remote staff use to reach operational support systems. - SonicWall advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 as reflected in the CVE record; CVSS per CISA enrichment; Defused and Previdian data via SecurityWeek and The Hacker News; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Advisory 6–7 Oct 2026; attempts from 8 Oct 2026; reported 12 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s 22–29 October ICS releases are light for rail: ICONICS SCADA products with three legacy lines that will never be fixed, two Hitachi Energy devices, EPICS Base and a video encoder
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS releases of 22, 27 and 29 Oct; no transport label; no reported exploitation
item.description: Beyond its republication of Siemens’ October advisories, covered in the Siemens card below, the CISA ICS advisories we could confirm for the window are six. ICSA-26-300-02 (27 October) republishes Mitsubishi Electric’s ICONICS advisory 2026-006 of 15 October: CVE-2026-16438, an incorrect privilege assignment rated CVSS v3.1 9.1, two weak password-recovery flaws (CVE-2026-16436 at 8.1 and CVE-2026-16437 at 6.4) and the libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 (8.2), across GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI, IoTWorX, MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz. GENESIS 11.04 and release 10.98 of the GENESIS64 family fix them, but no fix is planned for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz, which Mitsubishi Electric says should be replaced; meanwhile it advises replacing the password-recovery challenge file with a blank one and restricting write access to it. ICSA-26-300-01 (27 October) covers four network-reachable flaws in EPICS Base 7.0.10 and earlier, the open-source control toolkit used at accelerators and research facilities, including an integer overflow rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 / v4.0 9.3 (CVE-2026-114595); 7.0.11 fixes them. ICSA-26-295-01 (22 October) covers nine flaws in the Kiloview E3 video encoder, fixed in firmware 1.30. On 29 October CISA added three more. ICSA-26-302-02 covers Hitachi Energy TRO600 series firmware: CVE-2026-106087 lets an unauthenticated attacker read or download arbitrary files, including configuration and password data (CVSS v3.1 7.5 per CISA, v4.0 8.7 per Hitachi Energy), and CVE-2026-10756 lets an authenticated attacker use port forwarding to reach services bound to localhost (v3.1 7.5); 9.2.2.1 fixes both. ICSA-26-302-03 covers Hitachi Energy CoreTec 4 and 5: an authenticated command injection (CVE-2026-13162) and, on CoreTec5, the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-43284, for which public exploit code exists. CISA lists CoreTec5 5.0.0 as the fix and migration to CoreTec5 for CoreTec4, but the CVE record also lists 5.0.0 as affected, so check Hitachi Energy’s notice. ICSA-26-302-01 republishes Siemens’ Mendix SAML module advisory, a replay flaw rated CVSS v3.1 6.8. CISA lists Critical Manufacturing, not transportation, for the two 27 October advisories and Energy for the two Hitachi Energy advisories, and reports no known exploitation for any of the six. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: ICONICS software turns up as the HMI and energy-monitoring layer in facilities, including stations, depots and control buildings, and unfixable legacy lines are exactly what lingers in long-lived installations; Hitachi Energy equipment can sit in the substations that feed traction power, so the two Hitachi Energy advisories are worth a check even without a transport label. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-295-01, ICSA-26-300-01, ICSA-26-300-02 and ICSA-26-302-01 to -03, read via CISA’s CSAF data as mirrored by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; Mitsubishi Electric advisory 2026-006; KEV status per the CISA catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release) via CIRCL; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Mitsubishi Electric advisory 15 Oct 2026; Kiloview advisory 22 Oct 2026; ICONICS republication and EPICS Base advisory 27 Oct 2026; Hitachi Energy and Mendix republications 29 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 20 October ICS batch: a WAGO controller flaw that turns a low-privileged login into root, and Windows CAN-bus drivers that can be crashed — both labelled for transportation
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS release of 20 Oct, two transport-labelled items, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA published five ICS advisories on 20 October, and two list Transportation Systems among the sectors using the affected products. ICSA-26-293-02 republishes WAGO’s CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-096 for controllers on WAGO’s Linux-based firmware below 4.10.0 (FW32): CC100, PFC100 G2, PFC200 G2, TP600, Edge Controller and WP400. CVE-2026-80466 lets a low-privileged remote user inject operating-system commands through routing parameters in the web-based management, which a root helper then runs (CVSS v3.1 8.8); CVE-2026-88850 lets low-privileged users change root-owned PROFIBUS parameters (v3.1 8.1). Firmware 4.10.0 (FW32) fixes both. ICSA-26-293-01 covers six local flaws in HMS Networks’ PEAK-System PCAN Windows CAN drivers, 5.1.2 and earlier, that can crash the Windows kernel; the highest, CVE-2026-103672, is v3.1 7.1, driver 5.1.4 fixes them, and CISA says they are not remotely exploitable. The batch also covers Moxa’s AIG-302 edge gateway, where a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVE-2026-109813, v3.1 8.1 / v4.0 8.6) is fixed in 1.4.1, plus two Hitachi Energy revisions. None is reported exploited. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: WAGO sells a PFC200 XTR variant it describes as ideal for the railway industry and its controllers are common in building services, while PCAN adapters are a usual way to connect a maintenance laptop to a vehicle’s CAN network. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-293-01, -02 and -03, read via CISA’s CSAF data as mirrored by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; WAGO product page for the PFC200 XTR railway variant; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 20 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA republishes Siemens’ October advisories and the S7 PLC web-server flaws (CVSS 9.6) still have no fix — alongside October’s Rockwell ArmorBlock takeover and RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW fixes
item.category: Advisory — Siemens October advisories republished by CISA on 22 Oct, several still unfixed; Rockwell and Schneider fixes; no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA republished Siemens’ October advisories on 22 October as ICSA-26-295-02 to -18, including the exploited Software Center flaw covered in its own card above, and several products still have no fix: the S7 PLC web server across 157 listed S7-1500, ET 200SP and related products, where Siemens says it is preparing fixes; the GNU/Linux subsystems of the S7-1500 CPU 1518(F)-4 PN/DP MFP and the TM MFP module (though for the KEV-listed kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300, covered in its own card above, Siemens lists V3.1.7 as the fix for MFP V3.1.6); WinCC V7.5; and APOGEE MBC/MEC and Desigo PXC/PXM building controllers, for which no fix is planned. CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors. Siemens published the originals on 13 October, 17 new advisories by SecurityWeek’s count. The most serious, SSA-591731, covers eight web-server flaws in SIMATIC S7-1500, ET 200SP and ET 200pro CPUs and drive controllers, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6 by Siemens: an attacker can run code in an authorised user’s browser and perform PLC operations with that user’s rights. All versions are affected and only mitigations are available so far. SSA-832641 fixes authenticated path-traversal flaws in Industrial Edge devices (up to CVSS v3.1 9.1), with no fix yet for SCALANCE LPE9413 and LPE9433 or the affected HMI panels; SSA-784472 lists 377 CVEs in the optional Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 TM MFP technology module, also unfixed. SSA-508506 covers 11 flaws in RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW, including SQL injection and retrieval of administrator credentials, up to CVSS 8.8, fixed in V6.0. Rockwell’s only new advisory, SD1801, covers 1732E ArmorBlock I/O modules at 3.012 and earlier: CVE-2026-12655 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) lets an unauthenticated attacker change the web-server password and take over the module, and CVE-2026-12656 is a network-storm denial of service that needs a power cycle to clear; 3.013 fixes both. Schneider Electric issued SEVD-2026-286-02 for Sage RTUs that do not sufficiently verify firmware authenticity, fixed in C3414-500-S02L0, and SEVD-2026-286-01 for an unmaintained third-party component in Pro-face STW6000 and Harmony STW6 HMIs. None of these is reported exploited or listed in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: S7-1500 and ET 200SP controllers are common in depot, workshop, tunnel-ventilation and station plant; APOGEE and Desigo controllers run building heating and ventilation; CROSSBOW is built to manage remote access to substation devices, a model traction-power estates also use; and RTUs of the Sage type can sit in traction-power and pumping SCADA. - CISA ICSA-26-295-02 to -18 (22 Oct 2026), read via CISA’s CSAF data as mirrored by CIRCL; Siemens ProductCERT SSA-591731, SSA-832641, SSA-784472 and SSA-508506; Rockwell Automation SD1801; Schneider Electric SEVD-2026-286-01 and -02; advisory count per SecurityWeek; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Siemens advisories 13 Oct 2026; reported 14 Oct 2026; CISA republication 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 6–15 October ICS advisories: an end-of-life building controller and a camera platform labelled for transportation, both unfixable, plus N-Tron switches and Ignition
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS releases 6–15 Oct, two transport-labelled items with no fix, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA published ICS advisories on 6, 8, 13 and 15 October. Two list Transportation Systems among the sectors using the affected products, and neither has a fix. ICSA-26-279-01 republishes Johnson Controls’ JCI-PSA-2026-12 for EasyIO FG controller firmware: hard-coded credentials (CVE-2026-27872) and improper privilege management (CVE-2026-27873), each CVSS v3.1 7.7. The product is end-of-life, no fix will be issued, and Johnson Controls advises migrating to EasyIO Neo; CISA notes high attack complexity and that the flaws are not remotely exploitable. ICSA-26-288-02 covers Guangzhou Juan IoT’s EseeCloud app and firmware, used in low-cost IP cameras and recorders: hard-coded credentials at CVSS 9.8 (CVE-2026-107617) plus two medium flaws, and the vendor did not respond to CISA. Beyond the transport label, ICSA-26-281-01 covers seven flaws in Red Lion N-Tron 700 Series industrial Ethernet switches reported by Idaho National Laboratory, including factory administrator credentials that stay active, unauthenticated SNMP configuration changes and unsigned firmware updates (highest CVSS v3.1 8.3; the authentication bypass needs physical access); firmware 3.11.1 fixes them, and CISA updated the scores on 15 October. ICSA-26-286-01 covers a privilege-escalation flaw in Inductive Automation’s Ignition SCADA platform (CVE-2026-92817, CVSS v3.1 8.8), fixed in 8.1.55 and 8.3.9, and ICSA-26-288-01 six flaws in the open-source Eclipse Milo OPC UA library, fixed in 1.1.5 with no fix for the 0.6.x line. For energy, ICSA-26-279-06 covers Hitachi Energy’s end-of-life RTU500 CMU firmware, where CVE-2026-8065 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) allows unauthenticated firmware upload; the remedy is moving to supported firmware 12.7.8 or 13.9.1. CISA reports no known exploitation for any of them, and none is in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: EasyIO-class controllers run station heating, ventilation and lighting; low-cost camera platforms turn up at depots and car parks; N-Tron switches carry plant-room networks; Ignition is a common SCADA and HMI layer for station and facility systems; and RTU500 units can sit in traction-power substations. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-279-01, -279-06, -281-01, -286-01, -288-01 and -288-02, read via CISA’s CSAF data as mirrored by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; CISA bulletin of 8 Oct 2026; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 6, 8, 13 and 15 Oct 2026; N-Tron advisory updated 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager and Fortinet FortiMail join KEV as exploited zero-days — one configures the routers at every station and depot, the other screens mail into the corporate side
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, SD-WAN control plane and mail gateway
item.description: Cisco published an advisory on 30 September for CVE-2026-76504 in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager: improper handling of URI encoding lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker get past an authentication rule meant to protect an API endpoint and reach administrative-level access. Cisco scores it CVSS 9.8, offers no workaround, and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September; CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 3 October deadline, and Cisco revised the advisory on 2 October. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1, and releases older than 20.9 must migrate to a fixed one. On 1 October Fortinet disclosed CVE-2026-104286 in FortiMail (FG-IR-26-175), a path-traversal and NULL-byte handling flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the appliance through crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Fortinet scores it CVSS 9.8 and says it has been reported exploited in the wild; CISA added it to KEV on 1 October with a 4 October deadline. Affected are FortiMail 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1; Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2, and tells 7.2 customers to move to 7.4 or later. Neither vendor has named an actor or victims, and nothing ties either flaw to rail; Lumen’s Silent Train report, this edition’s top story, ties Volt Typhoon to an earlier Catalyst SD-WAN zero-day, CVE-2026-20127, not to CVE-2026-76504. The rail fit is our editorial assessment: SD-WAN Manager is the controller that pushes configuration and policy to the edge routers in stations, depots, yards and wayside communication huts, so administrative access there is a route to rewriting segmentation at every site at once; FortiMail sits on the corporate side, where a compromised mail gateway can read, alter or send the messages that open most intrusions against dispatch and operations staff. - Cisco advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU (revised 2 Oct 2026); Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-175; CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release); reported by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Cisco advisory and KEV listing 30 Sep 2026; FortiMail disclosure and KEV listing 1 Oct 2026; Fortinet fixed-release update 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 29 September and 1 October ICS batches lean on transport: a Lantronix cellular gateway whose firmware checks can be defeated, IP cameras at CVSS 10.0 with public exploit code, and an EV-charging platform with no version fix
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batches, transport-labelled devices, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA published seven ICS advisories on 29 September (ICSA-26-272-01 to -07) and six on 1 October (ICSA-26-274-01 to -06), and more than half of them list Transportation Systems among the sectors using the affected products. The one closest to rail infrastructure is ICSA-26-272-01, for the Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateway: firmware 2.6.0.4R6_stable carries an improper verification of cryptographic signature flaw (CVE-2026-91191) and a cross-site scripting flaw (CVE-2026-84409), each CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4 7.7, which CISA says could allow an attacker to replace software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. Version 2.6.0.7R6 fixes both, and CISA names Transportation Systems, Energy, and Water and Wastewater as the sectors. ICSA-26-272-03 covers command injection in VIVOTEK camera firmware across 37 models (CVE-2026-22755, CVSS v3.1 10.0 and v4 9.3), for which public proof-of-concept code exists; the fix is current firmware. ICSA-26-274-02 covers every version of Monta’s monta.app EV-charging platform, where missing authentication on a WebSocket interface allows charging-station impersonation (CVE-2026-95102, CVSS v3.1 9.4 and v4 9.3); there is no fixed version, only Monta’s guidance to enable OCPP 1.6 Security Profile 2 and its statement that rate limiting is in place. ICSA-26-274-01 covers Armatura One physical access control below 4.7.2 (USA builds below 4.6.1), which embeds an ActiveMQ component carrying CVE-2023-46604 — a flaw already in KEV from attacks on other ActiveMQ deployments, though none is reported against Armatura — plus hard-coded keys and credentials; 4.7.2 and 4.6.1_USA fix it. The other transport-labelled items are the Viidure dashcam Android app, with hard-coded cloud credentials (CVSS 10.0) and no fix planned; two lower-scored, fixed Johnson Controls EasyIO Neo controller flaws; and Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT terminal-management software, with a CVSS 10.0 flaw fixed in 7.8. CISA reports no known exploitation for any advisory in either batch. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: cellular gateways of the G520 type backhaul crossings, wayside cabinets, substations and vehicle telemetry; IP cameras and access control sit in every station; and transit agencies electrifying bus fleets run depot charging platforms of exactly the Monta type. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-272-01 to -07 and ICSA-26-274-01 to -06, details checked against CISA’s CSAF data as ingested by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 29 Sep 2026 and 1 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Two critical lwIP flaws in two weeks — the MQTT client on 22 September, the SMTP client on 6 October — and the question is still which field devices ship them
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS advisories, embedded TCP/IP stack, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA has now published two critical advisories for lwIP, the lightweight open-source TCP/IP stack built into a very wide range of embedded controllers, gateways, I/O modules and sensors. On 6 October ICSA-26-279-02 covered a classic buffer overflow in the SMTP client application of lwIP 2.2.1 (CVE-2026-15340, CVSS v3.1 9.8 per the advisory and v4.0 9.3 per the CVE record); the fix is an upstream patch and commit rather than a new release, and CISA names energy and water as the sectors. It follows ICSA-26-265-01 on 22 September, an out-of-bounds write in lwIP’s MQTT client (CVE-2026-87121, CVSS 9.8 v3.1 and 9.3 v4.0, network-reachable with no authentication or user interaction) that may give an attacker full code execution on the device; it was reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay. A separate double-free advisory published the same day, ICSA-26-265-02, was reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security; we could not verify its CVE or score, so none is quoted. Because lwIP is a library, exposure depends on whether a device maker compiled in the affected client application, and no downstream vendor list has been published for either flaw. The 22 September batch also carried two Siemens advisories that touch station estates: an unrestricted file upload in Siveillance Control, Siemens’ physical-security management platform, and a code-injection flaw in the Desigo CC building-management family, reported by Michelin CERT. No exploitation is reported for any of these. For rail, the plausible lwIP carriers are the telemetry gateways, condition-monitoring sensors and small controllers in traction-power, tunnel-ventilation and wayside cabinets, many of which publish over MQTT or send alarm email. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-279-02 as mirrored by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; ICSA-26-265-01 and -02 and the 22 Sep 2026 batch as listed by Chemical Facility Security News; CVSS for CVE-2026-87121 per the published CVE record (Ubuntu CVE tracker); rail-device relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 22 Sep 2026 and 6 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Rockwell extends its lockout-recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850, and MITRE now catalogues the PLC-tampering campaign behind it as C0066
item.category: Advisory — Vendor hardening and recovery guidance, revised
item.description: Rockwell Automation published revision 5.0 of security notice SD1790 on 18 September, its fifth revision since the notice first appeared on 30 July. The notice exists because of an FBI public service announcement of 30 July describing attackers who remotely altered the configuration of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, changed IP addresses and set passwords where none had existed, locking the operators out. The original guidance covered MicroLogix 1100 and 1400; revision 5.0 extends the hardening and password-recovery instructions to the Micro820 and Micro850 controllers as well. There is no CVE: the notice is about exposure and configuration, not a software flaw. The controls Rockwell lists are the familiar ones — remove the controller from any internet-reachable path, put access behind a VPN and firewall, set strong passwords, keep offline backups of the project so a locked controller can be restored, disable the built-in HTTP server and keep firmware current. The revision adds no new incident data. MITRE has since documented the July 2026 intrusions behind that PSA as campaign C0066 in ATT&CK v20 (page created 8 October, updated 13 October): more than 30 Minnesota municipal water and wastewater utilities whose internet-facing MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers had IP addresses and passwords changed, with program logic altered at one or more victims; MITRE says the campaign has not been formally attributed. Our assessment of the rail relevance: MicroLogix and Micro800-class controllers are the low-cost PLCs that end up in small, distributed installations built by contractors — pump and drainage stations, tunnel and station plant, yard equipment, small traction-power auxiliaries — often with a cellular modem for remote support and no entry in the operator’s OT asset register. The FBI describes a class of attack that needs no exploit at all, just reachability. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790 revision 5.0, referencing the FBI public service announcement of 30 Jul 2026; MITRE ATT&CK campaign C0066; rail installation pattern is our editorial assessment - Revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026; original notice 30 Jul 2026; MITRE C0066 created 8 Oct and updated 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s four-year strategy, “CISA 2030”, puts operational technology and consequence-based prioritisation at its centre — with a review of core services due to start within 60 days
