item.category: Regulation & Policy — CISA four-year strategy; OT named as a priority; no new obligations
item.description: CISA released its strategic plan, CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, on 26 October. Acting Director Nick Andersen describes a shift from passive defence to an anticipatory stance, and the plan says the agency will move away from threat-agnostic, all-hazards approaches toward risk-informed, consequence-based analysis. It names OT security — asset visibility and intrusion detection — among its priorities, alongside third-party and supply-chain guidance and support for a national risk register. CISA will begin a review of its core services within 60 days, deliver an implementation plan with metrics within 180 days and report progress after a year. The plan creates no new legal authorities and no new obligations for operators. Analysts quoted by GovInfoSecurity question how quickly the agency can deliver it with reduced staffing. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: a consequence-based CISA is likely to start conversations by asking which systems would hurt most if lost, and operators who have already ranked their own — dispatch, signalling support, traction power, passenger information — will be better placed in those conversations and in their TSA assessments. - CISA strategic plan as reported by Cybersecurity Dive, Nextgov/FCW, CyberScoop and GovInfoSecurity (cisa.gov could not be fetched); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Released 26 Oct 2026; core-services review to begin within 60 days

item.title: [Info] The OT Cybersecurity Coalition asks CISA for a binding directive on federal agencies’ own OT — a proposal, landing days after GAO found only 7 of 22 civilian agencies fully meet the device rules already in place
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Industry proposal for a federal OT directive; GAO audit
item.description: The OT Cybersecurity Coalition, an industry group, published a paper on 6 October, reported by CyberScoop, urging CISA to issue a binding operational directive dedicated to operational technology at federal civilian agencies. It asks that the directive make each agency assign an accountable OT cybersecurity officer, set minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, align with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and consider whether past NSA OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. In the coalition’s words, “it is time for an encompassing BOD solely focused on OT security.” Earlier directives (BOD 23-01, 23-02 and 26-04) touched OT without being dedicated to it. The coalition cites GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September, which reviewed 22 civilian CFO Act agencies against OMB requirements for networked IoT and OT devices: 15 had established inventories, 11 maintained them, 10 included all required information, and only 7 fully met all three. GAO notes that OMB has yet to issue updated guidance covering fiscal year 2026 and recommends that it do so. CISA did not respond to CyberScoop and has announced no such directive. On 14 October, after the French supermarket refrigeration attack, the coalition said failures in cybersecurity fundamentals had led to a significant incident, repeated the French cyber agency’s advice on VPN-only access, default passwords and firmware, and renewed its call for the directive, while noting that no US incidents of that kind have been reported. A directive of this kind would bind federal civilian agencies only — not railroads, transit authorities or their contractors. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: federal directives tend to become the reference for what regulators and auditors later expect of operators, and the requirements the coalition lists — a named OT owner, an inventory that is maintained rather than compiled once, minimum practices tied to the performance goals — are the ones TSA assessments already probe. - OT Cybersecurity Coalition paper as reported by CyberScoop; coalition statement as reported by Industrial Cyber; GAO-26-108937; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - GAO report 30 Sep 2026; coalition paper 6 Oct 2026; coalition statement 14 Oct 2026, reported 16 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s “Securing the Next 250” campaign boils critical-infrastructure advice down to reduce, replace, recover — and “replace” means the end-of-support kit railways keep longest
item.category: Regulation & Policy — CISA awareness campaign, voluntary
item.description: CISA has launched Securing the Next 250 for Cybersecurity Awareness Month, a voluntary campaign aimed at critical-infrastructure owners and operators, state and local governments and individuals, reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. Its organising idea is three Rs: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, and recover quickly to sustain operations. For individuals it repeats four practices: avoid and report phishing, use strong and unique passwords, turn on multifactor authentication and password managers, and keep software updated. Acting Director Nick Andersen framed the campaign around the knock-on effect a disruption has on the businesses and communities that depend on vital services. The campaign creates no new obligation and does not single out transportation. It is here because the three Rs map unusually well onto rail estates, where equipment lifecycles run to decades: reduce is the internet-facing remote-access and edge gear driving this page’s threat level, replace is the unsupported operating systems and network devices left in signalling support, passenger information and station plant, and recover is the manual-working plan that keeps trains moving when those systems are lost. That reading is our editorial assessment. - CISA Cybersecurity Awareness Month campaign, as reported by Industrial Cyber; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Reported 2 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] GAO’s industry panel says overlapping cyber-reporting rules pull responders away from containment — and CIRCIA’s final rule, logged for White House review on 1 October, remains pending
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Incident reporting burden, GAO panel report
item.description: GAO published GAO-26-109197 on 28 September, Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them. It records a virtual panel held on 16 July 2026 with six industry representatives from energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health, who said it could be difficult to satisfy every reporting requirement while also remediating a threat, and who saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector-specific ones. Half of the participants agreed that progress on harmonisation has been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency such as CISA to coordinate reporting; and closer government–industry collaboration. The report makes no formal GAO recommendations, and no rail or transit participant is listed. It follows analysis published on 8 September by the McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, citing earlier GAO work, that counted 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which reach private industry. The rule that would add another federal clock, CISA’s CIRCIA final rule, carried a September 2026 target in the federal regulatory agenda; the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs logged it for review on 1 October, and we found no published final text as of 31 October, when reginfo.gov still showed it pending review, so its 72-hour incident and 24-hour ransom-payment reporting duties are not yet in force and could still change. Rail sits in an unusually crowded corner of this map: a single event at a transit authority can trigger the 72-hour report to CISA required under the TSA security directives, an FTA or state safety oversight notification, a local emergency-management report and a breach notification if rider or payment data is involved — and, once it is final, CIRCIA as well. - GAO-26-109197; McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis via Industrial Cyber; CIRCIA status from the OIRA review record on reginfo.gov and HIPAA Journal; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - GAO report 28 Sep 2026; McCrary analysis 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule received for OIRA review 1 Oct 2026
